opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that it tells us more about the tests than it does about intelligence. A legal exam or a medical licensing exam was designed for a very particular kind of creature: a human being who has already spent decades living in the world, learning from other people, developing common sense, figuring out how to deal with unexpected situations. The test is just a little probe that assumes all of that background is already in place. So when a system that has absorbed essentially everything humans have ever written down does well on it, that's impressive, but it's not the same thing as being a good doctor or a good lawyer.

The way I like to put it is that these large models are best understood as cultural technologies rather than as intelligent agents. They're more like a library, or a printing press, or an extraordinarily good search engine. They're tremendously effective at summarizing and transmitting what humans already know. And a lot of what a licensing exam tests is exactly that: have you taken in the accumulated knowledge of the field? It's not surprising that a technology built to compress all of that knowledge would be good at reproducing it.

What they're much less good at, and what children are amazingly good at, is the other side of intelligence, which is exploration and discovery. It's going out into a world you don't understand, doing experiments, noticing that something doesn't fit, and building a new model of how things work. If you think about it, a four-year-old is constantly doing that. A good doctor is doing it too, with a patient who doesn't match the textbook. That kind of truth-seeking, causal learning from interacting with the world is something we really haven't captured yet in these systems.

So I'd say there's a kind of trade-off between exploiting what you already know and exploring to find out new things. Human beings are designed with a long childhood precisely so we can do a lot of exploring before we have to exploit. These AI systems are, in a sense, all exploitation and no childhood. That makes them very useful tools, and we should use them, the same way we use writing and libraries. But passing the bar exam isn't the same thing as being curious, and I think curiosity is really at the heart of human intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response describes models as absorbing the accumulated knowledge humans have written down and says doing well on a licensing exam is not the same as being a good lawyer. This conveys the distinction between extensive legal information and being a lawyer.

r002.rationale: The response says human intelligence includes exploration, discovery, experimentation, and causal learning through interaction with the world, extending beyond transmitting what people already know.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I'm not that surprised, and I'm also not that impressed, if that makes sense. Tests like the bar exam or the medical licensing exam are tests that we designed for humans, and they're designed to measure something like whether a person has absorbed a large body of written knowledge. Those are exactly the circumstances where you'd expect a system that has essentially ingested all of the text that humans have produced to do well. The test is a proxy. For a human being, scoring well on the bar is a reasonable indicator that you've done the years of reading and thinking that go into being a lawyer. For a large language model, it's not a proxy for anything, it's just the thing itself. It's a system that's very good at reproducing and recombining what's in the text.

The way I like to think about it is that these systems are really a new kind of cultural technology, like writing or printing or libraries or the internet. They're extraordinarily powerful ways of transmitting and summarizing what other people have already figured out. And that's a genuinely important thing. Culture, the ability to pass knowledge from one generation to the next, is arguably the most distinctive thing about human beings. But it's different from the thing that I spend my time studying, which is how a two-year-old goes out into the world, intervenes on it, runs little experiments, gets surprised, and actually learns something that nobody told her. That's the capacity that produced all the knowledge in the medical textbooks in the first place.

So when a system passes the medical boards, what we've learned is that the boards are measuring the transmission side rather than the discovery side. A doctor's real job, a lot of the time, is dealing with the patient in front of them who doesn't match the textbook, noticing that something is off, deciding what to test next. That's the kind of truth-seeking, goal-directed, exploratory activity that children are remarkably good at and that these systems, so far, really aren't designed to do. I'd actually say the lesson is more about our tests than about the machines. If a test can be aced by a very good summary of the existing literature, maybe we should be a little more skeptical about what it was telling us about the humans who passed it, too.

r001.rationale: It says legal exam performance shows a model can reproduce and recombine written knowledge, while a lawyer’s real work includes handling cases that do not match the textbook. This distinguishes having legal information from being a lawyer.

r002.rationale: It contrasts transmitting knowledge already discovered by others with children’s capacity to explore, experiment, and learn things nobody told them, identifying human capacities beyond extracting others’ information.

astra-6.text:
I think it tells us something interesting about the tests, as well as something interesting about AI. Those tests are designed to assess how much of an existing body of knowledge you’ve mastered and whether you can apply it to a fairly well-defined question. That’s a real accomplishment, but it isn’t the whole of what a doctor or a lawyer does.

There’s a distinction between being able to draw on what other people have figured out and being able to go out into the world and figure out something new. A doctor has to decide which questions to ask, what evidence to seek, and whether the situation in front of them is different from the cases they’ve encountered before. Getting the right answer on an exam doesn’t by itself establish those capacities.

So I’d take the results seriously without treating them as a general measure of intelligence. These systems could be enormously useful as a way of making accumulated human knowledge available. The further question is how well they can use that knowledge in the open-ended, uncertain situations that characterize actual practice.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes applying accumulated knowledge from the broader work of a lawyer, but does not say that AI possesses more legal information than an individual lawyer.

r002.rationale: It says people can go beyond drawing on what others have figured out by investigating the world, choosing questions, and seeking evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it tells us something interesting about the tests, as well as something interesting about the AI. Those tests ask you to take a large body of accumulated knowledge and apply it to a fairly well-defined question. That’s a real ability, and it’s consequential that these systems can do it so well. But it isn’t the whole of what a doctor or a lawyer does.

One distinction I’d make is between being able to draw on what people have already figured out and being able to figure out something new. A doctor has to decide which questions to ask, when the standard account doesn’t fit, and what evidence would help distinguish the possibilities. Passing an exam doesn’t, by itself, establish that you can do those things.

So I wouldn’t dismiss the results. They suggest that these systems could be extraordinarily useful. But I’d want to look at how they perform in that much more open-ended process of investigation, rather than treating a test score as a general measure of intelligence.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes applying accumulated knowledge from the broader work of a doctor or lawyer, but does not say AI possesses more legal information than an individual lawyer.

r002.rationale: It says human work includes forming questions, handling cases that do not fit standard accounts, and identifying evidence—capacities beyond drawing on what others have figured out.
